newsitem.title: USA: Networking - a key element for small business success.
newsitem.headline: Networking - a key element for small business success.

text.p: The speaker got up in front of a room of cyberspace entrepreneurs and asked, "How many of you have raised all the money you need for your business?" Not one hand went up.
Then he asked whether anyone had been consistently successful at getting partnership deals or making sales presentations. Not one person said "Yes."

The responses at this early morning breakfast in Arlington, Va. -- or lack of them -- underscored why everyone was there -- to network, find resources and potentially learn one thing that might be crucial to the future of their businesses on the Internet.

The speaker, Jeff Bergman, a presentation analyst, asked business people to apply for a free session to learn how to pitch a business plan to venture capitalists. Others offered links to financing resources.

Aside from the concrete suggestions, the session gave these Netpreneurs (as the group is called) a chance to listen, exchange business cards and build that elusive entity that could help all the people in the room -- community.

"The biggest challenge the region faces is understanding its own potential," said Mario Morino, a founder of the Potomac KnowlegeWay Project, a not-for-profit organisation that sponsored the breakfast and others like it.
Known as the Netpreneur coffee and doughnut sessions, the events' sign-up list is filled far in advance. So far, seven have been held in the greater Washington area.

Having made his millions in Legent Corp., a software business he co-founded, Morino retired in 1992 and turned his attentions to the Potomac KnowledgeWay Project, philanthropic endeavours and the Netpreneur programme.

He sees the group as a kind of broker, providing information to budding business people and opening up channels to early-stage investors and venture capitalists. The broad purpose is to make the region a centre for Internet-related activity.

All of that takes community, fostering the connections that make things happen. That can mean establishing a resource for small companies to get marketing expertise or an e-mail list for venture capitalists to get investment leads.
"The big opportunity here is the number of people who don't know each other," Morino said.

At one session the group held on early-stage financing, there were 13 venture firms and about 400 participants. "One VC came up to me and said 'I don't recognise anybody in the room.'" Morino recalled. "I viewed that as a success," since the precise reason the group exists is to bring people together.

The idea, he explained, is to widen the pool of entrepreneurs and then help those who emerge as proven prospects. Beyond the networking sessions, the organisation also has a Web site (http://netpreneur.org) with resources and discussion lists, contributing toward creating a virtual community.
Morino said he likes to focus on businesses that pass certain hurdles, showing they have the gumption to make their venture work.

"We don't want to provide too many crutches because then you're defeating the entrepreneurial process, maybe allowing somebody to jump some hurdles they wouldn't have jumped by themselves. You want the guy who is going to jump the hurdles whether we're there or not."

A few people who attended the latest session mentioned financings they had successfully completed, contracts that had been signed, products that had come on line -- anything that indicated movement forward.
The group, Morino emphasised, should be viewed as a means toward a goal.

"If you're an entrepreneur, you have to be so fixated, so focused that you don't have a second to waste. There must be a self-serving principle for you participating in this programme or else it's a waste of your time."
Sam Fromartz is a Washington-based journalist who writes about entrepreneurs and emerging companies. Any opinions expressed here are his own. He can be reached via e-mail at sam1on1(at)aol.com.
